title: When words run out
job: Paraphrase, ask what something means, repair a misunderstanding
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE INDEFINITE PARTICLES, and this is the last piece of grammar the ladder teaches. -to marks a thing that EXISTS but is unidentified to the speaker: Ya chto-to slyshal, I heard something — there was a definite something. -nibud' marks a thing not yet picked out at all, which is why it lives in questions, requests and futures: Skazhite chto-nibud', say anything. The series is regular across chto, kto and gde, so one law buys six words.

THE CIRCUMLOCUTION FRAME. Eto takaya shtuka, kotoraya … is L3-M9's relative pronoun doing the job it was really bought for: describing the thing when the name for it will not come. takaya and kotoraya agree with the noun, so a feminine shtuka takes both in -aya. L3-M9 opened this pronoun and wrote every form of it except this one, so the feminine nominative gets its own row here and points back there.

THE REPAIR MOVES, in order of how much they undo. to yest' restates what you just said (that is …). ya imeyu v vidu names what you MEANT — a frozen four-word phrase built on having in view, and vidu is a form that exists nowhere else. drugimi slovami reaches for a whole second phrasing. Povtorite, pozhaluysta hands the turn back. None of them is an apology and none needs one.

ENGLISH HELPS MORE HERE THAN ANYWHERE IN THE LEVEL: some- and any- split along nearly the same line as -to and -nibud' — something happened against did anything happen — so the mapping is free. It fails twice. Under a negative English says any (I didn't see anything) where Russian takes its negative series and NOT -nibud'. And English I mean is a verb of meaning, while ya imeyu v vidu is frozen, so the word-for-word attempt produces nothing at all.

THE SOCIAL RULE, which is the one that keeps a conversation going. An English speaker apologises before asking what a word means. In Russian the bare question is normal — Chto znachit eto slovo? — and an apology in front of it reads as distress rather than as manners. Ask, get the word, carry on.

sentences.display: Éhto takáya shtúka, kotóraya vsegdá rabótayet.
sentences.script: Это такая штука, которая всегда работает.
sentences.cue: It's the sort of thing that always works.
sentences.literal: This such thing, which always works.

words.note: Such a, of a feminine noun. It sets up the description that follows: takáya shtúka, kotóraya … — the sort of thing that … .
A thing, when you cannot name it. Feminine, slightly casual, and the single most useful noun a learner without a vocabulary can have.
The feminine nominative of L3-M9's kotóryy. It agrees with the noun it describes, not with the clause after it, so a feminine shtúka takes kotóraya.

sentences.trap: English can leave the relative pronoun out — the thing that works, the thing works. Russian cannot: kotóraya is compulsory and it must agree with shtúka.
sentences.sound: shtúka is SHTOO-ka. kotóraya is ka-TO-ra-ya, stressed on the second syllable, and the ending is said -aya, two vowels.

variations.changed: the frame with the description cut off, which leaves the listener nothing

variations.cue: It's the sort of thing that works.
variations.changed: the relative clause cut to its shortest

mistake.display: Éhto takóy shtúka, kotóryy vsegdá rabótayet.
mistake.script: Это такой штука, который всегда работает.
mistake.why: masculine forms on a feminine noun. shtúka is feminine, so both the setup and the pronoun end in -aya: takáya shtúka, kotóraya.

sentences.usage: The move that keeps a conversation alive when the noun will not come: describe it instead.
sentences.mnemonic: shtúka plus kotóraya buys you any noun you have forgotten.

words.note: What does … mean. Taken whole, because a tap on znáchit alone would give L4-M2's so-then; inside this pair the verb means mean.
A word, neuter. Front-stressed in the singular, SLO-va; the plural slová moves the stress to the end.

sentences.trap: English asks what does X mean with a do. Russian has no auxiliary here, and no apology in front: the bare question is the polite one.
sentences.sound: znáchit is ZNA-chit, front-stressed. The whole question falls at the end like a statement.

variations.changed: the same question about a word from this module
saying you lack the word instead of asking what it is

mistake.why: slóva is the plural, or the genitive of one word. The question asks about a single word standing in the nominative: éhto slóvo.

sentences.usage: Asking outright, mid-conversation, with no apology and no metalanguage.
sentences.mnemonic: Chto znáchit … ? is four syllables and buys you any word in the language.

words.note: Is called. Reflexive: the thing calls ITSELF, so no one is doing the calling and the -sya is not optional.

sentences.trap: English asks what is it called, with a passive. Russian asks HOW it calls itself — kak, not chto, and a reflexive verb with nobody doing the calling.
sentences.sound: nazyváyetsya is na-zy-VA-yet-sa; the final -tsya is said -tsa, with no y in it.

variations.changed: the question without po-rússki on the end
the thing named rather than pointed at

mistake.why: the -sya dropped. Without it the verb needs somebody doing the calling; with it the thing calls itself, which is what the question is asking.

sentences.usage: Pointing at an object and getting its name. The most economical sentence in the module.
sentences.mnemonic: Russian asks HOW a thing calls itself: kak … nazyváyetsya.

words.note: Something that exists but that you cannot identify. The -to half marks the existence; drop the hyphen and you have two unrelated words.
A sort of, and it takes the GENITIVE: vróde rabóty. It hedges the comparison, which is exactly what you want when the real word is missing.

sentences.trap: English a sort of takes a plain noun. vróde takes the GENITIVE, so rabóta becomes rabóty — the hedge costs an ending.
sentences.sound: vróde is VRO-dye, front-stressed. chto-to is SHTO-ta, with the chto said sh and the clitic unstressed.

variations.changed: the hedge without chto-to in front of it
the same particle marking a real something the speaker cannot name

mistake.why: the dictionary form left standing. vróde governs the genitive, so it is vróde rabóty, the same ending L5-M6's v techéniye takes.

sentences.usage: Naming a thing by what it resembles when the real word is gone.
sentences.mnemonic: vróde eats a genitive: vróde rabóty, never vróde rabóta.

sentences.cue: That is — I didn't get it.

words.note: That is. Two owned words taken whole, because a tap on yest' alone would give L1-M7's there is, which is true of the word and false of the pair.
Got it, past tense, masculine. A woman says ponyalá. Ya ne ponyál is the ordinary way to say that a sentence did not land.

sentences.trap: The first word is to, not éhto. They look alike on the page and only to belongs in this pair; éhto yest' is not a phrase.
sentences.sound: to yest' is said ta-YEST', run together, with the stress on the second word.

variations.changed: the repair restating a fact instead of confessing
the confession without the repair marker in front of it

mistake.why: éhto for to. The pair is frozen as to yest'; éhto yest' would be this exists, and the repair meaning is gone.

sentences.usage: Repairing your own sentence, or admitting the other person's did not land.
sentences.mnemonic: to yest' is one phrase: a tap on yest' alone gives you there is, which is not what you said.

sentences.display: Ya iméyu v vidú, chto éhto trúdno.
sentences.script: Я имею в виду, что это трудно.
sentences.literal: I have in view, that this hard.

words.note: I mean — four words frozen into one phrase, literally I have in view. vidú is a form that exists nowhere else, and the phrase never breaks apart.

sentences.trap: English I mean is one verb, so the word-for-word attempt reaches for a verb Russian does not use this way. The Russian is four frozen words about having something in view.
sentences.sound: The phrase runs as ya i-MYE-yu v vi-DOO, with the stress at the very end on vidú.

variations.display: Ya iméyu v vidú éhto slóvo.
variations.script: Я имею в виду это слово.
variations.changed: a noun after the phrase instead of a clause

variations.display: Ya iméyu v vidú, chto éhto vázhno.
variations.script: Я имею в виду, что это важно.
variations.changed: the same frame over a different claim

mistake.display: Ya iméyu v vid, chto éhto trúdno.
mistake.script: Я имею в вид, что это трудно.
mistake.why: vid for vidú. The -ú ending here exists only inside this phrase; the dictionary form never appears in it, and the phrase never comes apart.

sentences.usage: Correcting a misunderstanding about what you meant, rather than about what you said.
sentences.mnemonic: Russian does not mean things, it has them in view: iméyu v vidú.

sentences.cue: In other words, it's very simple.

words.note: In other words. Both words are instrumental plural and they agree, so it is drugími slovámi and never drugíye slovámi.

sentences.trap: English in other words is three words that never change. The Russian is two instrumentals that agree with each other, so getting one ending wrong breaks the pair.
sentences.sound: drugími slovámi is dru-GEE-mi sla-VA-mi, both words stressed on their second-to-last syllable.

variations.changed: the same repair with the opposite verdict
the restatement alone, with nothing marking it as one

mistake.why: drugíye is the nominative plural. Both halves of this phrase are instrumental and must match: drugími slovámi.

sentences.usage: Reaching for a second phrasing when the first one clearly failed.
sentences.mnemonic: Two instrumentals that travel together: drugími slovámi.

sentences.cue: I didn't catch that, could you say it again.

words.note: Caught what was said. The ras- prefix is the difference from slýshal: not hearing at all is slýshal, not catching it in a noisy room is rasslýshal.
Say it again — the polite plural imperative. With pozháluysta it is a request; without it, still perfectly civil.

sentences.trap: English apologises first — sorry, I didn't catch that. In Russian the bare statement plus the request is normal, and an apology in front of it sounds like distress.
sentences.sound: rasslýshal is ras-SLY-shal with a doubled s you can hear. povtoríte is pav-ta-REE-tye.

variations.changed: the request alone, which is enough by itself
the reason alone, which a Russian already hears as the request

mistake.why: slýshal says you did not hear at all, which in a conversation is nearly an accusation. rasslýshal says the room was noisy, which is what you mean.

sentences.usage: Keeping your turn when the sentence arrived and did not survive the journey.
sentences.mnemonic: ras- is the noisy room: slýshal is deafness, rasslýshal is a bad line.

words.note: Anything at all, nothing picked out yet. It belongs in questions, requests and futures, and never after a negative.

sentences.trap: English any under a negative — I didn't say anything — tempts a learner into ne … chto-nibud'. Russian never does that; -nibud' lives in questions, requests and futures only.
sentences.sound: chto-nibud' is shto-ni-BOOD', stressed at the end, and the chto is said sh as always.

variations.changed: the request without pozháluysta
the -to twin, where the thing said exists and is simply not named

mistake.why: English any dragged under a negative. A negated Russian clause takes the negative series instead; -nibud' after ne is not said at all.

sentences.usage: Asking somebody to speak when it does not matter what they say.
sentences.mnemonic: -nibud' asks, -to tells: Skazhíte chto-nibud', Ya chto-to skazál.

sentences.display: Ya gde-to éhto slýshal, i kto-to éhto skazál.
sentences.script: Я где-то это слышал, и кто-то это сказал.
sentences.cue: I heard that somewhere, and somebody said it.
sentences.literal: I somewhere this heard, and somebody this said.

words.note: Somewhere — a real place you cannot name. L1-M7's gde with the same -to clitic, and the whole is one token.
Somebody — a real person you cannot name. The last member of the series, and it takes the same endings as kto.

sentences.trap: English somewhere and anywhere are close enough to blur. Russian keeps them apart by whether the thing EXISTS: a place you were in is gde-to, never gde-nibud'.
sentences.sound: gde-to is gdye-TA and kto-to is KTO-ta; in both, the clitic is unstressed and the host keeps its weight.

variations.changed: the first half, with the place left unidentified
the second half, where the somebody exists but is not named

mistake.why: -nibud' in a past statement. You were somewhere when you heard it, so the place exists and takes -to; -nibud' would mean anywhere at all, which cannot be true of something that happened.

sentences.usage: Reporting a half-remembered fact without pretending to a source you do not have.
sentences.mnemonic: It happened, so it happened somewhere: past tense takes -to.

comprehensionPool.script: Это такая штука, которая всегда работает.
comprehensionPool.cue: It's the sort of thing that always works.
That is — I didn't get it.

comprehensionPool.script: Я имею в виду это слово.

comprehensionPool.cue: In other words, it's very simple.
